title: Nero's tutor
hookLine: Seneca taught and advised Nero, and his record at court is still debated

cards: The year is 49. Seneca has spent eight years exiled on Corsica, a rocky island he described as bare and harsh, sent there by the emperor Claudius on a charge of adultery with a princess. Then a message arrives.
Agrippina, the emperor's new wife, wants him back in Rome. She has a son, a boy of about twelve, and she wants one of the most admired writers in Rome to teach him. The boy's name is Nero.
Saying yes ends the exile. It also ties Seneca's name, forever, to one of the most notorious rulers Rome ever had.

teach.b: First, the good years. When Nero became emperor at sixteen, Seneca and the soldier Burrus steered the young ruler, and later Roman writers remembered his first years as a decent stretch of government.

Seneca wrote him a book, On Clemency, urging mercy as the mark of a great ruler. Second, the speechwriter. Seneca wrote Nero's speeches, including the funeral praise for Claudius, the emperor who had exiled him.
Many scholars also think he wrote a cruel satire mocking that same Claudius. Third, the darkest night. In 59, Nero decided to kill his own mother.
Tacitus says Seneca and Burrus were called in; Seneca looked at Burrus and asked whether the soldiers should be ordered to do it.
Afterward, a letter to the Senate justifying the murder was widely believed to be Seneca's work. Tacitus doesn't tell us what Seneca felt, and no one can. Fourth, the way out that wasn't.
In 62 Burrus died, and Seneca asked to retire and offered his fortune back. Nero refused, with warm words. Seneca withdrew anyway, as far as he could.
Three years later he was ordered to die. So what was he doing at court? One reading: staying to restrain a dangerous man, and doing some good.
Another: staying for power and wealth, and lending his name to crimes.
Many historians see some of both: a man in a room with no clean exits, making hard compromises, some of them very wrong.

how: Students of Seneca usually read his life alongside Tacitus' account and treat his years at court as an open moral question about staying inside power to restrain it.

games.q: you're Seneca in 49, exiled on Corsica. the empress offers a way home, if you'll teach her son. what do you do?
o: go back and teach the boy.
go back but refuse any role at court.
games.why: he went back, and the choice tied his name forever to Nero.

practice: Think of a compromise you've made, at work, in a family, in a friendship, going along with something to keep a place at the table.
Hold both sides honestly, what good staying did and what it cost, without rushing to a verdict, the way historians hold Seneca. If there's a line you wouldn't cross, name it quietly to yourself now.

wordCard.voice: Nero's tutor. Seneca taught the boy, guided the young emperor, and stayed close through crimes. His record is still argued. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'mercy': the title of the book Seneca wrote to the young emperor Nero.

carryVoice: Your line: hard compromises. Some of both is the honest place to leave him. See you tomorrow.
